q: A bakery's price rises 10% and the quantity demanded falls 5%. What does this say about demand?
r: It is inelastic
Quantity changed by a smaller percent than price.
w: That needs quantity to fall by more than the price rose.
That would mean buyers vanish with any price rise.
That needs the percent changes to be equal.

q: Price elasticity of demand is calculated by dividing the percent change in quantity demanded by:
r: The percent change in price
This ratio shows how sensitive buyers are to price.
w: Supply is not part of this formula.
Costs are not part of this formula.

q: Quantity demanded falls 20% when price rises 10%. What is the price elasticity of demand?
r: 2, so demand is elastic
20 divided by 10 equals 2, which exceeds 1.
w: The percent changes are not equal.
This is not the result of the division.

q: Which factor makes demand for a good more elastic?
r: Many close substitutes are available
Buyers can easily switch when the price rises.
w: The good is a basic necessity with no alternative
The good takes up a tiny part of the budget
Small purchases make buyers less sensitive to price.
Buyers have very little time to react

q: What is income elasticity of demand for a normal good?
r: Positive, because demand rises as income rises
Buyers purchase more when they earn more.
w: Negative, because demand falls as income rises
Zero, because demand never responds to income
Normal goods do respond to income.
Infinite, because every buyer spends all of it
This is not a property of normal goods.

q: What is an inferior good?
r: A good people buy less of as their income rises
Instant noodles are a common example.
w: A good that is of poor quality and cannot be sold
Inferior refers to demand, not defects.
A good that people buy more of as income rises
A good whose price never changes at all
Price stability does not define it.

q: What is cross-price elasticity used to show?
r: How demand for one good responds to another good's price
Substitutes and complements react differently.
w: How supply of a good responds to its own price
That is price elasticity of supply.
How income affects how much people save
How prices differ between two countries

q: The price of tea rises and demand for coffee increases. What does this suggest about tea and coffee?
r: They are substitutes
Buyers switch to coffee when tea costs more.
w: A change in demand shows a link.
Income is not what changed here.

q: What does price elasticity of supply measure?
r: How much quantity supplied responds to a price change
Flexible producers have more elastic supply.
w: How much quantity demanded responds to a price change
That is price elasticity of demand.
How much costs respond to output changes
How much profit responds to taxes

q: Why is supply usually more elastic in the long run than in the short run?
r: Producers have time to expand capacity
Factories and workers can be added over time.
w: Producers have less time to change output
Prices stop affecting what producers do
Costs fall to zero over a long period

q: What is a price floor above equilibrium likely to create?
r: A surplus of the good
Sellers offer more than buyers want to buy.
w: That follows a ceiling below equilibrium.
A perfect balance of supply and demand
A fall in the quantity supplied
Quantity supplied rises at the higher price.

q: Who bears more of a tax placed on a good when demand is inelastic and supply is elastic?
r: Buyers bear most of the tax
They cannot easily cut back, so prices rise for them.
w: Sellers bear most of the tax
Elastic sellers can shift away, so they bear less.
The government bears the tax cost
No one bears the tax at all

q: What is consumer surplus?
r: The gap between what buyers would pay and what they pay
It measures the benefit buyers gain from a market.
w: The gap between price and the cost of making a good
The total money spent in a market
The extra goods left unsold on shelves

q: What is producer surplus?
r: The gap between the price received and the cost of making a good
It measures the benefit sellers gain.
w: The gap between what buyers would pay and what they pay
The unsold goods left in a warehouse
The money producers spend on materials

q: A buyer would pay $12 for a meal but pays $9. What is the buyer's consumer surplus?
r: $12 minus $9 equals $3.
w: That is the maximum willingness to pay.

q: Which concept says that rational people compare extra benefits with extra costs?
r: Thinking at the margin
Choices depend on the next unit, not the average.

q: What does the circular flow model show?
r: How money, goods and resources move between households and firms
Households supply resources and firms supply products.
w: How prices rise in a spiral over time
How a single firm decides its output
How taxes move in one direction only

q: In the circular flow, what do households sell to firms?
r: Labor and other resources
Firms pay wages, rent and interest in return.
w: That is not a core flow.

q: What is a production possibilities frontier (PPF)?
r: A curve showing the most of two goods an economy can make
Points on it use all resources efficiently.
w: A line showing the price of two goods
A graph of a firm's yearly profit
A list of resources a country owns

q: What does a point inside the production possibilities frontier mean?
r: Resources are underused or inefficient
The economy could make more of both goods.
w: The economy is using resources at full capacity
That would be on the frontier.
The economy has more resources than possible
That would be outside the frontier.
The economy has stopped producing anything
That would be at the origin.

q: What does a point outside the production possibilities frontier show?
r: An output level that is unattainable with current resources
Growth is needed before the economy can reach it.
w: An output level that is easy to reach today
An output level that wastes resources
Waste is shown inside the curve.
An output level with no opportunity cost

q: What would shift a country's production possibilities frontier outward?
r: Better technology or more resources
Capacity to produce rises.
w: A fall in the number of workers
A rise in the price of imports
A decision to make more of one good

q: What is economic growth?
r: An increase in an economy's output over time
It is often measured by real GDP.
w: A rise in prices across the economy
A fall in the number of jobs
A rise in government spending only
That is one part of GDP.

q: Which factor most directly raises long-run economic growth?
r: Increases in productivity
Each worker produces more with better tools and skills.
w: That does not raise output by itself.

q: What is human capital?
r: Workers' skills, knowledge and experience
Education and training increase it.
w: Money that people keep in savings accounts

q: What is physical capital?
r: Tools, machines and buildings used in production
Firms invest in it to raise output.

q: What is the unemployment rate formula?
r: Unemployed divided by the labor force
It is shown as a percent.
w: Unemployed divided by the total population
The labor force is the base.
Employed divided by the labor force
Labor force divided by the unemployed

q: A discouraged worker has stopped looking for a job. How is this person counted?
r: Not in the labor force
Only active job seekers count as unemployed.
w: They do not have a job.
As part of the labor force

q: What is frictional unemployment?
r: Short-term joblessness while people move between jobs
It exists even in a healthy economy.
w: Joblessness caused by skills no longer needed

q: What is the natural rate of unemployment?
r: The rate that remains when the economy is at full employment
It includes frictional and structural unemployment.
w: The rate during a deep recession
That is above the natural rate.
It is not set by law.

q: What is cost-push inflation?
r: Rising prices caused by higher production costs
Firms pass on costs like wages and materials.
w: Rising prices caused by too much spending
Falling prices caused by weak demand
Rising prices caused by a stronger currency
A stronger currency usually lowers prices.

q: What is demand-pull inflation?
r: Rising prices caused by demand that outpaces supply
Too much spending chases too few goods.
w: Rising prices caused by higher production costs
Falling prices caused by lower demand
Prices that stay constant despite demand

q: Who tends to lose most when inflation is unexpectedly high?
r: Lenders who receive fixed payments
Repayments are worth less than expected.
w: Owners of real estate whose value rises
Asset values tend to rise with prices.

q: What is the money multiplier effect?
r: Bank lending expands the money supply beyond the initial deposit
Loans become new deposits that are lent again.
w: Banks refusing to lend any deposits
That would shrink the money supply.

q: What is a reserve requirement?
r: The share of deposits banks must hold rather than lend
The Fed can set it to influence lending.
w: The share of loans banks must make each year
That is not a reserve rule.
The tax banks pay on deposits
That is not a reserve rule.
The fee customers pay for opening accounts

q: What is the discount rate?
r: The interest rate the Fed charges banks that borrow from it
It influences banks' borrowing costs.
w: The interest rate banks charge each other overnight
That is the federal funds rate.
The interest rate on home loans
The price cut on sale items

q: What are open market operations?
r: The Fed buying and selling government securities
They change the amount of money in the banking system.
w: Banks opening branches in new markets

q: If the Fed buys government securities from banks, what happens to the money supply?
r: It increases
Banks receive cash they can lend out.
w: That would follow a sale of securities.

q: What is the Phillips curve about?
r: The trade-off between inflation and unemployment
In the short run lower unemployment often means higher inflation.
w: The trade-off between taxes and spending
The trade-off between imports and exports
The trade-off between saving and borrowing

q: What is a government budget surplus?
r: Tax revenue exceeding government spending in a year
The extra can reduce debt.
w: A rise in the national debt

q: What is crowding out?
r: Government borrowing raising interest rates and reducing private investment
Borrowers compete for a limited pool of savings.
w: Too many shoppers filling a store
That is not the economic idea.
Firms forcing rivals out with low prices
Banks refusing to lend to the government

q: What is a progressive tax system?
r: Rates rise as income rises
Higher earners pay a larger percent.
w: This is not a tax system.

q: What is an automatic stabilizer?
r: A policy that cushions the economy without new legislation
Unemployment benefits and progressive taxes are examples.
w: That is not an economic tool.
A law passed during each downturn

q: Why do unemployment benefits act as an automatic stabilizer?
r: They rise in recessions and support spending
Payments increase as more people lose jobs.
w: They fall in recessions and cut spending
They end when the economy slows

q: Which feature marks a command economy?
r: Central planners decide what to produce
The state sets output targets and often prices.
w: Customs guide who does which job

q: What is a key advantage of a market economy?
r: Competition pushes efficiency and innovation
Firms must serve buyers to survive.

q: What is a key disadvantage of a pure market economy?
r: It may leave some people without basic needs
Markets reward ability to pay.
w: It has no competition at all
Competition is a feature of markets.
It sets prices by central order
Prices come from supply and demand.

q: Which situation best fits a traditional economy?
r: Families pass down farming methods through the generations
Customs decide the roles and methods.
w: A government sets quotas for every factory
Firms compete using prices and advertising
A central bank sets interest rates
That is a monetary policy tool.
